title: Global Load Balancing
description: Explore anycast routing, GeoDNS with Route 53, multi-region active-active architectures, and how Netflix achieves global failover.

segments.text: So far we've balanced traffic within a single data center. But your users are global. A user in Tokyo hitting a server in Virginia adds two hundred milliseconds of latency from physics alone. Speed of light through fiber is about two-thirds c. You can't fix physics, but you can fix geography.

The first layer is GeoDNS. When a user resolves your domain, the DNS server checks the client's IP geolocation and returns the IP of the nearest data center. Route 53's latency-based routing goes further: it measures actual network latency, not just geographic distance, because network topology doesn't follow geography.

Anycast is more elegant. You advertise the same IP address from multiple data centers via BGP. The internet's routing protocol naturally sends each user to the nearest announcement. Cloudflare runs their entire CDN this way. One IP, two hundred cities, zero DNS-level decisions.

A Global Server Load Balancer, or GSLB, sits above your regional load balancers. It's the traffic cop for the planet. It monitors health across regions, knows capacity in each data center, and can shift traffic based on load, latency, or active incidents. F5 and AWS Global Accelerator serve this role.
segments.thought_prompt: What's the difference between routing users to the nearest region versus the healthiest region?

segments.text: Multi-region active-active means every region serves real traffic simultaneously. No standby regions burning money doing nothing. The hard part is data. If a user writes in us-east-1 and reads from eu-west-1 fifty milliseconds later, do they see their write? This is where consistency models collide with physics.

Active-passive is simpler but wasteful. One primary region handles all writes. Secondary regions replicate data and sit idle until failover. Recovery time objective: minutes, not seconds. You're paying for idle infrastructure, but you've eliminated cross-region write conflicts entirely.

Failover strategies range from manual to fully automated. DNS failover is slowest because of TTL propagation, sometimes minutes. BGP withdrawal is faster, around ninety seconds. The gold standard is health-check-triggered GSLB failover, which can redirect traffic in under thirty seconds.

Netflix runs active-active across three AWS regions: us-east-1, us-west-2, and eu-west-1. Their Zuul gateway handles regional routing. When us-east-1 had an outage in 2017, they evacuated the entire region's traffic in under seven minutes. Two hundred million streaming hours a day, and users barely noticed.

Their secret: stateless edge services with regional Cassandra clusters using eventual consistency. User data is replicated across all three regions asynchronously. They accept that a user might see stale recommendations for a few seconds after failover. That trade-off is worth one hundred percent availability.
segments.thought_prompt: Could a banking application use the same eventual consistency approach? Why or why not?

segments.text: Global load balancing is where networking, distributed systems, and business requirements intersect. GeoDNS for basic geographic routing, anycast for CDN-scale distribution, GSLB for intelligent failover. Choose your architecture based on your consistency requirements, not just your latency budget.
